content.thinking:
I'm tracing why reverting the flag at 14:45 didn't resolve the incident—the service stayed at incident level and was judged refuted, so the flag got switched back on, meaning the underlying fault is still active. I need to dig into the logs around the monthly-spend feature to understand why the revert wasn't effective.

Checking for earlier changes to rule out, I find only the two flag toggles (P1, P2) in the change history — no prior deploy or config change exists in the window, so there's nothing additional to exclude. I'll cite that deploy reads came back empty and replicas stayed on one revision, while noting the flag revert itself was already refuted as a fix rather than treated as a ruled-out cause.

For the division-by-zero mechanism, it rests entirely on F1: a shopper with zero purchases this month hits an empty list and divides by a length of zero, with no supporting S or D reading — so this reaches a cause but still relies on an unrun reading, even though the logged line number confirms location. The timing lines up exactly, with metric and log onset at 14:39:00 matching P1's flag flip.

For contributing factors, I'm noting that no test existed for the no-purchases summary path before the flag went live, which would have caught the fault pre-flip — now checking whether that's addressed by the existing test-coverage action item.

I'm drafting an item requiring flag-guarded paths to be tested with the flag enabled before production rollout, since CF-1 wasn't actually covered by prior items. For CF-2, the flag appears to have gone to full traffic almost immediately with no staged rollout or automatic error-rate halt, so I'm proposing a gradual rollout mechanism with an auto-halt guard. For CF-3, I'm weighing whether the delayed flag revert counts as a pre-existing factor or just part of the response, since only conditions present before the incident began should count as contributing factors.

Then for the paging gap, I'm noting that nobody being alerted is a finding worth its own contributing factor — the alert routing wasn't connected to on-call paging — so I'm proposing a fix to route HighErrorRate alerts for io-shop directly to on-call. I'm also tracing how the account page failure manifested for flagged shoppers at the io_shop boundary.

Moving to action items, I'm drafting a prevention measure requiring that tests exercise every flag-guarded path with the flag enabled, including the no-purchases-this-month shopper edge case, before that flag can be turned on in production.

I'm also separating out a staged-rollout idea into two distinct items: rolling out flags like the monthly-spend feature gradually to a small share of accounts first, and automatically halting or reverting a staged rollout when the account page's error rate spikes.

For routing, I want HighErrorRate alerts on io-shop to page on-call directly as its own item.

For the stop-the-harm piece, I need to confirm the fix actually propagates: not just toggling monthly-spend-feature off, but verifying at io-shop's own flag evaluation logs that it reads as off and that the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47 has actually stopped, since the earlier revert didn't reach the service evaluations.

I also need to explain why io-shop kept evaluating the flag as on through 14:46–14:47 even after the switch-off at 14:45:53 — whether there's a propagation delay or caching issue — while sticking only to what the record actually shows, without speculating.

For lessons learned: on the positive side, Argus reverted the flag after the alert was raised, the investigator correctly traced the onset to the flag change, and Code-Fix drafted a PR afterward — the mitigation agent's choice to toggle the flag when the revert didn't help was a solid design decision. Now I'm turning to what went wrong.

The Mitigation Agent judged the revert as refuted even though the service's own logs showed the flag still evaluated as on after the switch-off, so it dismissed that cause and restored the faulty flag. There's already a standing requirement that the Mitigation Agent confirm a change actually reached the service before judging it — that's worth flagging as a gap. I should also note that the second investigation arrived at the same candidate cause with no further input from Argus, and that nobody paged anyone, which I'm treating as a contributing factor too.

I also recall an earlier incident that tried reverting this same flag and was likewise refuted — suggesting the pattern repeated and Argus retried the same fix without verifying it actually took effect, which I should record as another contributing factor. Nothing stands out as a lucky break; latency and traffic were unchanged per the second investigation, but that's just a candidate detail, not worth logging as fact.

For assumptions, I'm noting that the incident's start time comes from the Investigator's placement, the customer-loss figure is a lower bound, the failing requests are assumed to be non-purchasing shoppers based on a single data source, and the earlier disconnect errors were treated as baseline. I'm keeping all these as named placeholders while I draft the causal chain, starting with how account pages failed for shoppers based on the error rate in the service log.

Now I'm filling in the next causal steps: the error rate spike figures, confirming flag evaluations were on during the relevant window, noting the revert attempt's logs still show the flag active afterward (so the "refutation" doesn't actually clear it), and finally detailing the mechanism — a spend-per-item calculation dividing by zero items purchased this month for shoppers who bought previously but not recently, which is the root trigger tied to the flagged code path.

In plain words, turning on the monthly spending summary feature likely caused the account page to divide by zero for shoppers who had purchased before but not within the current month.

I'm mapping this fault to contributing factor CF-1, the missing check, which has no other item addressing it yet, so my action item should cover that gap. I'm also considering the "nobody paged" factor—if someone had been alerted, they might have caught the issue sooner, though that's a more indirect mitigation than fixing the root cause.

Now I'm double-checking the write-up to avoid stray numbers, swapping references like "PR #400" for phrasing such as "the draft pull request" to keep things clean.

action_items.item: Require tests that run each flag-guarded path of io-shop with its flag on, including edge-case accounts such as a shopper with no purchases this month, to pass before that flag can be switched on in production.
Switch io-shop feature flags on in stages, starting with a small share of requests, rather than for all traffic at once.
Halt a staged flag rollout on io-shop automatically, and switch the flag back off, when the account page error rate rises above its baseline.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to on-call paging so a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages failed. The account page error rate the service logged reached {Gbac1.5}, against a typical {Gbac1.6}, and was highest at {Gbac1.7}. Across all requests the error rate was {errors_while_broken} while it was broken, against {errors_before} before.

Account page requests were failing with ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} of src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. This error first appears in the logs in the onset minute and continues through {G5309.3}. Before the onset, the account page errors logged were shoppers closing the connection.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: the change events read over the wider window came back with only the two flag toggles and no deploy.

causal_chain.step: The failing code runs on the path that monthly-spend-feature enables, and an admin switched that flag on at {P1.1}. Before then, every evaluation of the flag read off ({G7e5d.4}). In the minute it was switched on, {G971b.2} of {G971b.3} evaluations read on, and from then on every evaluation read on ({Gce95.4}). The failed revert does not clear the flag. The flag was switched off at {P2.1}, but the service kept logging the flag as on in the minutes after that, so the switch-off was not seen to reach the service.

On the path the flag enables, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` builds the list of items bought this month and divides the month's total by the length of that list. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, the list is empty, so the division raises ZeroDivisionError. The log names the same line.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new monthly spending summary on shoppers' account pages likely made the page divide by zero for shoppers who had bought before but nothing this month, so their account pages failed.

contributing_factors.factor: Before monthly-spend-feature was switched on in production, no check was seen that ran the path the flag enables against a shopper who had bought before but nothing this month.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have failed in the check, before the flag was switched on for shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for every account page request within a minute. No staged rollout and no automatic halt on a rise in errors was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of requests would have reached the failing path, and the rise in errors could have stopped the rollout before it reached all traffic.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to on-call paging, so nobody was paged.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been engaged once the alert was raised and could have seen that the service still logged the flag as on after it was switched off, rather than the incident ending with the flag back on.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well: The Investigator placed the onset in the same minute that monthly-spend-feature was switched on, and named the failing line from the logs.
Argus switched off the flag that set it off {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Code-Fix opened a draft pull request for a person to review {T39.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
went_wrong: The revert was judged refuted while the service's own log lines still showed monthly-spend-feature evaluated as on after the switch-off. The flag was put back on, and the incident ended with the triggering change still in place.
Argus's memory held an earlier incident in which the same flag revert had been refuted. The revert was tried again without first checking whether such a switch-off reaches the service.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, `render_spend_summary` calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the shopper's spend this month by the number of items bought this month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, that number is zero, so the division at line {F1.1} raises ZeroDivisionError and the account page request fails.
input.still_at_risk: With monthly-spend-feature back on and the division unchanged, account pages for shoppers who bought nothing this month would likely keep failing.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again. Confirm at io-shop itself that its flag-evaluation log lines read monthly-spend-feature=off and that the ZeroDivisionError lines at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py stop: after the earlier switch-off, the service's lines still read on.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
input.why_it_did_not_help: Find out why io-shop kept logging monthly-spend-feature as on after the flag provider switched it off at {P2.1}, and whether that switch-off ever reached the service's flag evaluation. If it did reach it, find out why account page requests kept failing.
